title: Percentile-driven soft backpressure and request bucketing to stabilize microbatching at sustained QPS
creator: Alyssa Chen
description:
Goal: Implement a percentile-driven soft backpressure mechanism plus request bucketing to reduce microbatch variance and prevent GPU OOM/latency spikes at sustained high QPS while preserving throughput. This ticket scopes the design, initial prototype, experiments, and rollout plan.

Background:
- We observe that under sustained high QPS (>= 4k req/s per worker for certain seq-length distributions) the microbatch size distribution becomes bimodal: long tails of tiny batches (~1-2 tokens) interspersed with large batches. This increases GPU memory churn due to frequent KV cache allocations and forces the scheduler to oversubscribe device memory, leading to occasional OOM kills and P95 latency spikes.
- Prior work (ENG-16234, ENG-14902) implemented hard ceilings and eviction heuristics; those reduce OOMs but create throughput cliffs and poor latency for latency-sensitive customers.

Proposal summary:
1) Percentile-driven soft backpressure: rather than a single hard cap on admission, measure the moving window of microbatch sizes and GPU memory pressure and compute a dynamic admission probability based on the 90th/95th percentile of observed allocations and batch assembly time. Admission controller reduces acceptance probability smoothly as the target percentile approaches a safe threshold, avoiding abrupt drops.
2) Request bucketing by affinity: split incoming requests into buckets by expected token footprint (short, medium, long) and model variant affinity. Maintain separate microbatch queues and percentile metrics per bucket. This reduces head-of-line blocking where long-seq requests delay many short ones and vice versa.
3) KV-cache-aware trimming: when soft backpressure signals sustained pressure, perform low-latency KV trimming in two stages: a) speculative prefix eviction for cold keys (bucket-level LRU hints), b) compact in-memory KV slab consolidation before GC to reduce fragmentation. Both are conservative and aim to reclaim small amounts of GPU memory early to avoid hard eviction policies.
4) GPU tile-aware allocation: coordinate microbatch assembly with allocator to prefer packable tensor shapes, minimizing internal fragmentation. Use a packing hint from the admission controller when possible.

Tradeoffs and rationale:
- Smooth admission vs hard ceilings: smoother ensures graceful degradation for P50/P90 rather than cliff failure modes. It requires robust percentile estimation but reduces customer-facing incidents.
- Bucketing increases complexity (additional queues and metrics) but reduces variance across batches and better aligns batching strategies to request types.
- KV trimming risks slightly increased cold-cache misses; we mitigate with targeted heuristics: only trim keys with access gaps > N requests or low reuse score computed per bucket.

Success criteria (metrics to measure):
- Reduce GPU OOM incidents by >= 80% on overloaded experiments compared to current baseline.
- P95 latency under sustained high QPS should reduce by >= 30% (current is ~2.4x spike). P50 should stay within 10% of baseline.
- Throughput (tokens/sec) should not decrease more than 8% in steady-state workloads.

Implementation plan (phases):
A) Instrumentation & simulation (Week 1): add per-bucket microbatch histograms, moving-percentile estimator (P90/P95), and GPU allocator pressure hooks. Build a load simulator that can replay traffic traces with mixed seq-length distributions.
B) Admission prototype (Week 2): implement configurable soft-admit controller with tunable curve (linear, sigmoid, step) and wire into the front-door admission path. Feature-flag behind runtime.canary.soft_backpressure.
C) Bucketing + KV hints (Week 3): add request bucketing and per-bucket queues. Emit bucket-level metrics and attach lightweight LRU hints for KV entries.
D) KV trimming and packing hints (Week 4): integrate conservative KV trimming routine and allocator packing hints. Run forced-reclaim stress tests.
E) Canary rollout (Week 5): enable on 5% of traffic in staging and then 10%, evaluate metrics and regressions, iterate.

Experiment notes and initial results (so far):
- Small-scale sim (4 workers, 3k req/s sustained) with sigmoid soft-admit reduced variance of batch sizes (P95 microbatch size reduced from 48->26) and lowered allocator peak by ~22%.
- End-to-end staging run with bucketed short/long split shows short-bucket P95 latency improvement of ~28% while long-bucket throughput maintained within 4%.

Open questions / risks:
- Percentile estimator stability: need to choose smoothing window and guardrails to adapt to flash traffic bursts.
- Accurate bucket classification: misclassification (e.g., request with unknown tokenization) could harm packing efficiency. Consider lightweight tokenizer estimate in front-end.
- Interaction with multi-tenant dedicated pools: policies must respect tenant isolation and capacity reservations.

Next steps / tasks:
- [ ] Finalize admission probability curve and default params.
- [ ] Add integration tests for KV trimming with synthetic cold/warm access patterns.
- [ ] PR for instrumentation: runtime metrics + dashboards.
- [ ] Implement canary rollout plan and alert thresholds.
